title: 2022 surplus allocation and downtown police pilot funding
subtitle: Heritage study funding, Maltby Road wildlife crossing, e-scooter bylaw report, police board appointment and union agreement.
overview: Council allocated the 2022 operating surplus to reserves and grants, mostly to offset future tax pressure from inflation and growth revenue shortfalls linked to Bill 23 {{vote:m4}}. It also approved capital funding adjustments, including money for a permanent wildlife crossing and fencing on Maltby Road {{vote:m7}}.

Council approved $500,000 from the Growth Reserve Fund to speed up the Ward West Cultural Heritage Study and related heritage work, ahead of the Heritage Act deadlines tied to Bill 23 {{vote:m8}}. It also approved use of $260,000 from the Police Operating Contingency Reserve for the Guelph Police Service downtown initiative, a pilot {{vote:m10}}.

Staff were directed to report back on a bylaw to permit personal e-scooters at the July 5 Committee of the Whole meeting {{vote:m6}}. After the closed session, the Mayor said council had given staff direction to finalize and execute a memorandum of agreement with the union representing city employees. Council also appointed a new member to the Guelph Police Services Board in open session.

decisions.detail: Council allocated the 2022 operating surplus among reserves, reserve funds and grants, including transfers to infrastructure, growth, police and utility reserves.

decisions.item: Capital budget adjustments and Maltby Road wildlife crossing
decisions.detail: Council approved the capital funding adjustments and $375,000 from the Infrastructure Renewal Reserve Fund for a permanent wildlife crossing and fencing on Maltby Road.
Council approved $500,000 from the Growth Reserve Fund to expedite the Ward West Cultural Heritage Study and support heritage work tied to Bill 23 deadlines.
Council approved the Police Services Board request to use $260,000 of the Police Operating Contingency Reserve.
Staff must bring a report and draft Traffic Bylaw amendment on personal e-scooters to the July 5 Committee of the Whole, skipping normal pre-consultation and seeking police input.
Council received the Guelph Police Service Downtown Initiative report.

debate: On the heritage funding, a councillor said the current capacity would allow only about 10 to 15 individual designations before the Bill 23 deadline, and that studying whole cultural heritage landscapes would cover more properties and leave heritage staff time for designations.

The heritage funding was described as up to $400,000 for the study and $100,000 for a contract staff person. That person would handle public engagement on several projects, which would free heritage staff for designations.

One councillor asked how the police would address equity and the comfort of people uneasy around heavily uniformed officers downtown. Council members said this is an operational matter and suggested the question go to the police board chair or chief.

Supporters of the downtown pilot cited concerns from downtown businesses and residents about safety and gaps in mental health, addiction and housing supports. Another councillor said they felt safe downtown and cautioned against linking homelessness or addiction with an unsafe downtown or a police-only response.
Councillors noted the pilot is collecting data on interactions and outcomes, and that results will go back to the police board for review. The funding is from the police service's own reserve.
